summary:
Dead Reckoning is a browser game that lets students design, launch and fly a complete small-satellite mission, and then keep it alive when parts fail.

Players choose a mission goal, one of three real orbits (Sentinel-2A, NASA's Landsat 9, or the ISS) and a launch vehicle that sets their mass limit and spends from the same budget as their parts. They then build a CubeSat from seven subsystems while mass, cost, power, battery, data and pointing budgets update live, and the spacecraft assembles itself in 3D.

The six-hour mission is flown on the real orbit, computed from published orbital data, over Earth imagery from NASA GIBS, with space weather from NASA DONKI. Three failures strike during flight, and the recovery options depend on what the player built. The debrief traces every loss back to a decision and suggests specific changes for the next attempt.

Teams of up to four can share one screen, each player owning a subsystem and its failure. Mission design is a chain of trade-offs that students usually learn one at a time; Dead Reckoning makes them feel how one choice affects the rest.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Dead Reckoning walks a player through a whole space mission in four steps.

1. Brief: the mission, a timeline of the six-hour flight with its three scheduled failures, and a clear split between what is real data and what is modelled for play.

2. Design: choose a goal (imaging survey, wide-area mapping or precision science), an orbit, a launch vehicle, and seven subsystems: structure and data recorder, solar arrays, battery, radio, antenna, attitude control and science instrument, plus an optional backup beacon and a risk posture. Every choice changes mass, cost, power, eclipse battery margin, downlink capacity and pointing accuracy. A design that breaks a limit cannot launch, and each part bolts onto a 3D model as it is chosen.

3. Fly: the mission runs at 60x, 300x or 900x speed. The spacecraft captures twelve images and downlinks them during real ground-station passes over Wallops, Goldstone and Canberra. The main radio fails, then attitude control degrades, then the battery loses capacity. Each failure pauses the clock and offers recovery paths, and those paths are checked against the actual design: no backup beacon means no beacon option, and a coarse attitude system changes which images stay usable.

4. Debrief: a grade from F to S, a score split into science (60%), data (25%) and resource use (15%), a timeline linking each loss to the decision that caused it, a comparison table across runs, and up to four one-click changes for the next attempt, each re-checked against the budgets.

HOW IT WORKS

The orbit is propagated with the SGP4 model from published element sets (CelesTrak) for Sentinel-2A, Landsat 9 and the ISS. Sunlight, eclipse, ground track and station visibility are computed from that geometry every 10 simulated seconds, not scripted. Solar flares, geomagnetic storms and solar particle events from NASA DONKI become bounded penalties on power, pointing and sensor noise. Earth in the 3D view uses NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery and turns with real sidereal time, so the day-night line is the true one. Each data source shows whether it is live or a stored copy, and the game runs fully offline from bundled snapshots.

TEAM PLAY

One to four players share one screen. Four roles (mission lead, spacecraft engineer, communications, science and attitude) each own their parts and make the call when their subsystem fails. With fewer players, roles are shared.

FOR NEW PLAYERS

Every screen has a short first-run walkthrough. A built-in "Grade S plan" loads the best design we found for the default mission and explains why each part and each recovery decision wins, so beginners can learn from a complete example before trying their own.

WHY IT MATTERS

Students usually meet orbits, power budgets, communications and failure planning in separate lessons. In a real mission they are one connected problem: a bigger camera means more data, which needs a faster radio, which needs more power, which needs bigger arrays, which costs mass the launch may not allow. Dead Reckoning makes that chain visible and lets players test it again and again, with the same seed giving the same result so runs can be compared fairly in a classroom.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

Failures are not random events: the recovery options come directly from what the player built. The debrief explains cause and effect instead of only giving a score. The orbit is a real decision: the same design scores differently over Landsat 9 than over Sentinel-2A, because the passes and lighting differ.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Honesty about the model: every constant and rule is documented, and the app says plainly what is real and what is a teaching assumption. Reproducibility: no hidden randomness, so the same seed replays exactly. Accessibility: keyboard operable, readable contrast, works on phones. Reliability: offline snapshots, validation of all downloaded data, and a 2D fallback when a device cannot show 3D. There is no single right answer: every goal and orbit combination is playable, and the best possible grade changes with the orbit.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js with React Three Fiber for 3D, satellite.js for SGP4, Vitest for 115 automated tests. Static site, no backend.

CODE

https://github.com/PranavRaj-K/dead-reckoning

The spacecraft is fictional and this is an educational model, not a flight prediction tool. Not affiliated with NASA.
dataRefs: NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information)
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services), Blue Marble Shaded Relief and Bathymetry
Landsat 9 mission (orbit used as a playable reference orbit)
projectRefs: ESA Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission (Sentinel-2A orbit used as the default orbit)
CelesTrak GP orbital element sets (Sentinel-2A, Landsat 9, ISS)
TLE API (public mirror used to capture the Landsat 9 and ISS snapshots)
React Three Fiber (React renderer for three.js, MIT)
